summary: Defines a set of SNMP managed objects for monitoring and configuring traffic engineering in MPLS networks, such as the tunnels operators set up to steer traffic along chosen paths. It lets standard network management tools read and manage this state in a uniform way.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC describes a set of tables that network management software can read and write over SNMP to manage MPLS traffic engineering tunnels. It says what each table holds, which rows an operator creates to build a tunnel, and which objects need protecting so that only authorised managers can change them.

subtitle: The SNMP objects that let an operator create, inspect and monitor MPLS traffic engineering tunnels.

tldr.problem: An operator who builds traffic engineering tunnels needs a standard way to set them up and read their state with network management software.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a MIB module, a set of tables of managed objects, that describe tunnels, the hops they take, the resources they need and the traffic they carry, all reachable with SNMP.
tldr.outcome: The module was assigned the object identifier { mplsStdMIB 3 } and is meant to be used together with the companion MIB in RFC 3813.

today: RFC 3812 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It is meant to be used with the companion MIB in RFC 3813, and the module it defines was registered under the MPLS subtree as { mplsStdMIB 3 }.

sections.title: What This MIB Is For
sections.content:
The RFC defines a portion of the Management Information Base, the MIB, for use with network management protocols. In particular, it describes managed objects for modelling a Multiprotocol Label Switching traffic engineering system, and it is meant to be used together with the companion document RFC 3813 for MPLS traffic engineering configuration and management.

The management framework is the standard one. Managed objects are reached through a virtual information store, the MIB, and are generally accessed with SNMP. Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms of the Structure of Management Information, and this module is compliant with SMIv2, described in RFC 2578, RFC 2579 and RFC 2580.

The terminology follows the MPLS architecture. An explicitly routed LSP, also called a label switched path, is referred to here as an MPLS tunnel. It consists of one or more in-segments and out-segments at the ingress and egress routers, each segment being associated with one MPLS interface; these are also called tunnel segments. At a router in the middle of the path, a connection is modelled as one or more in-segments and out-segments, and the binding between them is performed with a cross-connect. Those objects are defined in the companion MIB, RFC 3813.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is the list of things a network device can be asked about and told to do over SNMP. This RFC adds the entries for traffic engineering tunnels, so that management software can work with any device that implements it.

sections.title: What the Module Has to Support
sections.content:
The module is designed to satisfy four requirements and constraints. It supports the configuration of point-to-point unidirectional tunnels. MPLS tunnels need not be interfaces, but it is possible to configure a tunnel as an interface.

It supports tunnel establishment by an MPLS signalling protocol, in which the tunnel parameters are specified with this MIB module at the head end of the path and the tunnel is established end to end by signalling. It also supports manually configured tunnels, in which the label associations at each hop are provisioned by the administrator through the LSR MIB in RFC 3813. Finally, it supports persistent as well as non-persistent tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: The module covers the two ways tunnels get built: the router can set the path up by signalling it, or an administrator can build it hop by hop. A tunnel is one-way and joins two points, and it may or may not look like an ordinary network interface.

sections.title: The Tables That Make Up the Module
sections.content:
The module is built from six tables. The tunnel table, mplsTunnelTable, is used to set up tunnels. It allows new tunnels to be created between an MPLS router and a remote endpoint, and existing tunnels to be reconfigured or removed. Only point-to-point tunnels are supported, although multipoint-to-point and point-to-multipoint connections are possible through a router acting as a cross-connect, so each tunnel can have one out-segment originating at a router and one in-segment terminating there.

The tunnel table does not define the in-segments and out-segments that form the tunnel. Those are defined by creating rows in the in-segment and out-segment tables, defining relationships in the cross-connect table, and referring to those rows from the tunnel table with a cross-connect index, mplsTunnelXCIndex.

The resource table, mplsTunnelResourceTable, indicates the resources a tunnel requires, such as rates and burst sizes. Several tunnels may share the same resources by pointing to the same row, while tunnels that do not share resources must point to separate rows. The hop tables come in three kinds. mplsTunnelHopTable gives the hops, strict or loose, for a tunnel that is established by signalling; each row carries a secondary index, mplsTunnelHopIndex, corresponding to the next hop, and the scalar mplsTunnelMaxHops gives the maximum number of hops that can be specified on each tunnel the router supports. mplsTunnelARHopTable gives the actual hops the tunnel traversed, as reported by the signalling protocol after the tunnel was set up; support for it is optional, since not every signalling protocol can report it. mplsTunnelCHopTable lists the hops computed by a constraint-based routing algorithm from the hop table for the signalling protocol in use, and its support is optional too.

The performance table, mplsTunnelPerfTable, augments the tunnel table with counters that measure tunnel performance: packets forwarded, a high-capacity version of that counter, packets dropped because of errors or other reasons, bytes forwarded, and a high-capacity version of the byte counter. The CR-LDP resource table, mplsTunnelCRLDPResTable, holds resource information for tunnels signalled with CRLDP, and is a sparse extension to the resource table indexed by the same index; it may be implemented only by devices that support the CR-LDP signalling protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The module is a set of tables. One holds the tunnels, one holds the resources they ask for, three hold the hops a tunnel takes, one holds the counters, and one holds extra resources for tunnels set up with a particular signalling protocol.

sections.title: When Counters Have to Be 64 Bits
sections.content: The module provides 64-bit counters for high-speed interfaces where 32-bit counters would be impractical. The rules, copied from RFC 2863, are these. For interfaces that operate at 20,000,000 bits per second or less, 32-bit byte and packet counters must be supported. For interfaces that operate faster than 20,000,000 bits per second and slower than 650,000,000 bits per second, 32-bit packet counters must be supported and 64-bit octet counters must be supported. For interfaces that operate at 650,000,000 bits per second or faster, both 64-bit packet counters and 64-bit octet counters must be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: A counter that only goes up to four billion wraps too soon on a fast link, so the module asks for wide counters once a link reaches a certain speed.

sections.title: Showing a Tunnel as an Interface
sections.content:
The Interfaces Group of MIB II defines generic managed objects for managing interfaces, and this RFC adds the media-specific extensions that let an MPLS tunnel be managed as a logical interface. It follows the interpretation in RFC 2863, under which each sub-layer below the internetwork layer of a network interface is considered an interface, so the MPLS interface appears as an entry in the interfaces table. The interface stack then looks like a tunnel interface of type mplsTunnel(150) sitting above an MPLS interface of type mpls(166), sitting above the underlying layer, which is the ifIndex of any interface type for which MPLS internetworking has been defined, such as ATM, Frame Relay or Ethernet.

Some entries of the interfaces table take particular meanings for a tunnel. Each tunnel is represented by an ifEntry, with ifDescr describing the tunnel and ifType set to 150. ifSpeed is the total bandwidth in bits per second for the tunnel to use. ifPhysAddress is unused. ifOperStatus reflects the real operational status of the tunnel and is down(2) when the tunnel is down. ifInOctets and ifOutOctets count the octets received and transmitted over the tunnel. ifInErrors counts labelled packets dropped because of uncorrectable errors, and ifInUnknownProtos counts received packets discarded during header validation, including packets with unrecognised label values. ifName is the textual name of the tunnel, unique on the system, or an octet string of zero length. ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable defaults to disabled(2), ifConnectorPresent is set to false(2), and ifAlias holds the non-volatile alias name given to the tunnel by a network manager.
sections.plainLanguage: A tunnel can also look like an ordinary interface, so that the same status and traffic counters work for it. The RFC says which of the standard interface fields carry what for a tunnel, and gives the tunnel its own interface type number.

sections.title: Example of Setting Up a Tunnel
sections.content:
The RFC walks through the objects an administrator would change to create a best effort, loosely routed, unidirectional traffic engineered tunnel across two hops of a simple network. The objects are created on the head-end router.

First, a row in the resource table describes the traffic the tunnel asks for, with the resource index, the maximum rate, the mean rate, the maximum and mean burst sizes and the weight. Then two rows in the hop table describe the hops. The first hop is the fictitious router 192.168.100.1, the head end, with address type ipv4(1), prefix length 32, hop type strict(2) and the path option name 'Here to there'. The second hop is the router 192.168.101.1 at the far end, with hop type loose(2) and the same path option name. Finally a row in the tunnel table ties it together, with the tunnel index, the tunnel instance, the ingress and egress router identifiers, the name 'My first tunnel' and the description 'Here to there', the cross-connect pointer, the signalling protocol set to none(1) for a manually built tunnel, and the hop table index pointing at the hop list.

Each row is activated with a RowStatus value of createAndGo(4), which creates the conceptual row and sets its status to active immediately; a later read returns active(1).

The pointers follow a convention called RowPointer, which identifies a conceptual row by pointing at the first accessible object in it. The tunnel table's mplsTunnelXCPointer points at the row in the cross-connect table that holds the LSP for that tunnel, and mplsTunnelResourcePointer points at the row of the traffic parameter table, such as the resource table, that holds the tunnel's traffic parameters. Both must point to the first instance of the first accessible columnar object, so that a manager can find the matching row. If mplsTunnelXCPointer returns zeroDotZero, it means no LSP is associated with that tunnel instance; if mplsTunnelResourcePointer returns zeroDotZero, no quality of service resource is associated with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Building a tunnel means creating rows in three tables: one for the resources it needs, one for each hop along the way, and one for the tunnel itself that points at the other two. Each row is created with a single status value that switches it on as it is written.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the module is useful for monitoring MPLS traffic engineering tunnels, but it can also be used to configure objects, and anything that can be configured can be configured wrongly with potentially disastrous results.

Several objects in the module have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create, and such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. Supporting SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations. The tunnel table, hop table, resource table and CR-LDP resource table collectively hold the objects used to provision tunnels, tunnel hops and tunnel resources, and unauthorised access to them could disrupt traffic on the network, especially for a tunnel that has already been established. The RFC says stronger mechanisms such as SNMPv3 security should be considered where possible, and specifically that SNMPv3 VACM and USM must be used with any v3 agent that implements this MIB. Administrators should also consider whether read access to these objects should be allowed, since read access may be undesirable in some circumstances.

Readable objects matter too. The tunnel, hop, resource, actual hop, computed hop, performance and CR-LDP resource tables collectively show the network topology of the tunnels and its performance characteristics, and should be treated as sensitive if an administrator does not want to reveal that information. Even encrypting the values over the network with SNMP is not enough on its own, because SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there was no control over who is allowed to read or change the objects.

The RFC therefore recommends that implementers use the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, including its cryptographic mechanisms for authentication and privacy, and states that deployment of SNMP versions prior to SNMPv3 is not recommended. It then leaves it to the operator to make sure that the SNMP entity giving access to the module is configured to give access only to the users who have legitimate rights to the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables that create tunnels are powerful, and a manager that can write them can disturb real traffic. The RFC insists on SNMPv3 with its access control and encryption, and warns that the readable tables reveal the shape of the network.

sections.title: Registry Assignment
sections.content: MPLS related standards track MIB modules should be rooted under the mplsStdMIB subtree, as described in the MPLS management document and as requested by the MPLS-TC-STD-MIB in RFC 3811. The RFC requests a new assignment under that subtree, which can only be made through a Standards Action. IANA has assigned { mplsStdMIB 3 } to the MPLS-TE-STD-MIB module specified in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: Every MIB module needs its own number in the tree of all MIB modules. This one was given the number 3 under the MPLS subtree.

data.title: Creating a two-hop tunnel
data.code:
mplsTunnelResourceTable
  mplsTunnelResourceIndex = 5

mplsTunnelHopTable
  hop 1: 192.168.100.1  strict (2)
  hop 2: 192.168.101.1  loose (2)

mplsTunnelTable
  mplsTunnelIndex = 1
  mplsTunnelIngressLSRId = 192.168.100.1
  mplsTunnelEgressLSRId = 192.168.101.1
  mplsTunnelIsIf = true (1)
  mplsTunnelRowStatus = createAndGo (4)
